# Reformed Worldview Evaluation

Reformed theologians would immediately note that **any educational model must be Christ- and God-centered**, not child- or skill-centered. As one commentator paraphrases Reformation teaching, “education’s primary goal should be to form an adult, not develop a child” – and child‑centered pedagogy tends to produce self‐centered adults[\[1\]](https://www.modernreformation.org/resources/articles/in-the-teachers-lounge-with-melanchthon-luther-and-calvin-exploring-education-with-the-reformers#:~:text=fostering%20the%20outward%20expression%20of,can%20be%20of%20help%20today). Indeed, the secular “child‐centered” mindset assumes children are inherently good and should freely explore, whereas Scripture treats children as sinners in need of **biblical instruction and discipline**[\[2\]](https://christcenteredcurriculum.com/article-god-centered-vs-child-centered/#:~:text=Children%E2%80%99s%20natures%20are%20sinful%3B%20restraint,is%20in%20order). Kevin Swanson himself argues that education must view the child as a *whole person* – **physical, emotional, and spiritual** – not merely a cognitive learner[\[3\]](https://store.generations.org/products/upgrade-4th-edition?srsltid=AfmBOorSTBloMwQaQYSlTT7NxKHI3W75QFxkbuKzQAVyGofGHcTEeX3O#:~:text=,true%20reality%20of%20the%20child). He emphasizes that “education is discipleship” – the fear of God and Christ’s lordship must undergird every lesson[\[4\]](https://store.generations.org/products/upgrade-4th-edition?srsltid=AfmBOorSTBloMwQaQYSlTT7NxKHI3W75QFxkbuKzQAVyGofGHcTEeX3O#:~:text=Summarized%20in%20this%20book%20are,yet%20profound%3A%20Education%20is%20discipleship).

Accordingly, labeling activities by developmental “domains” (cognitive, motor, etc.) is **not forbidden per se**, but Reformed critics would insist those categories serve *God’s purposes*, not secular ones. If “cognitive domain” means teaching mathematics through God’s providence, it can be embraced; but if it means abstract skills taught apart from Scripture, it is suspect. Swanson warns against narrowing education to the intellectual alone: “if a program addresses the child’s intellect while ignoring his spiritual and emotional development, it ignores the true reality of the child”[\[3\]](https://store.generations.org/products/upgrade-4th-edition?srsltid=AfmBOorSTBloMwQaQYSlTT7NxKHI3W75QFxkbuKzQAVyGofGHcTEeX3O#:~:text=,true%20reality%20of%20the%20child). Likewise R.C. Sproul reminds parents that the family – not secular schooling or the child’s whims – is the divinely ordained place to train children in God’s truth[\[5\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ultimately-with-rc-sproul/teaching-our-children-about-god#:~:text=The%20Lord%20has%20ordained%20the,significant%20responsibilities%20of%20Christian%20parents). In short, Reformed thinkers would **caution strongly** that any developmental‐milestone framework must be subordinated to *knowledge of God*. They would reject an activity model that treats learning as autonomous discovery; instead it must be explicitly tethered to Christ and Scripture from the outset[\[6\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ultimately-with-rc-sproul/teaching-our-children-about-god#:~:text=And%20if%20we%20read%20on%2C,Christians%2C%20now%20that%20terrifies%20me)[\[4\]](https://store.generations.org/products/upgrade-4th-edition?srsltid=AfmBOorSTBloMwQaQYSlTT7NxKHI3W75QFxkbuKzQAVyGofGHcTEeX3O#:~:text=Summarized%20in%20this%20book%20are,yet%20profound%3A%20Education%20is%20discipleship).

In practical terms, Swanson and others would likely *warn* against an uncritical developmental framing. The modern pedagogy’s assumption of innate child goodness (Montessori, Dewey, etc.) is at odds with Augustine/Calvin’s doctrine of total depravity[\[1\]](https://www.modernreformation.org/resources/articles/in-the-teachers-lounge-with-melanchthon-luther-and-calvin-exploring-education-with-the-reformers#:~:text=fostering%20the%20outward%20expression%20of,can%20be%20of%20help%20today). They would insist every activity point to God’s sovereignty: e.g. a counting game should celebrate God’s created order, and every physical skill (run, jump, draw) reflect Imago Dei creativity, not mere “self-actualization.” Developmental determinism (“wait till they’re ready”) would be viewed skeptically: Scripture shows children can grasp truth early (e.g. Eunice and Lois teaching young Timothy[\[7\]](https://www.9marks.org/review/family-driven-faith-voddie-baucham/#:~:text=On%20the%20edge%20of%20the,1%E2%80%939)). In sum, Swanson *would not* bless a purely secular “domain” chart. He would affirm structuring learning in areas *if* each domain is taught under Scripture’s lordship[\[3\]](https://store.generations.org/products/upgrade-4th-edition?srsltid=AfmBOorSTBloMwQaQYSlTT7NxKHI3W75QFxkbuKzQAVyGofGHcTEeX3O#:~:text=,true%20reality%20of%20the%20child)[\[6\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ultimately-with-rc-sproul/teaching-our-children-about-god#:~:text=And%20if%20we%20read%20on%2C,Christians%2C%20now%20that%20terrifies%20me), but he would **reject** any framing that sidelines the Gospel and God’s law.

## Family Sessions vs. Individualized Learning

Reformed tradition strongly affirms the **family (household)** as the God‑appointed unit of education. Jesus rebuked attempts to banish children from his teaching (“Let the children come to me… for to such belongs the kingdom of God” – Mark 10:14–15)[\[8\]](https://churchandfamilylife.com/resources/641236ecbee8e2ceb85e3cef/seven-reasons-to-attend-a-family-integrated-church#:~:text=,he%20took%20them%20in%20his), and the Apostles assumed children of believers would be present and taught at home and church[\[9\]](https://churchandfamilylife.com/resources/641236ecbee8e2ceb85e3cef/seven-reasons-to-attend-a-family-integrated-church#:~:text=,and%20instruction%20of%20the%20Lord)[\[6\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ultimately-with-rc-sproul/teaching-our-children-about-god#:~:text=And%20if%20we%20read%20on%2C,Christians%2C%20now%20that%20terrifies%20me). Voddie Baucham and Joel Beeke note that pre‑modern believers **catechized children within the family**, not in segregated Sunday schools[\[7\]](https://www.9marks.org/review/family-driven-faith-voddie-baucham/#:~:text=On%20the%20edge%20of%20the,1%E2%80%939)[\[10\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=During%20the%20Reformation%20and%20particularly,at%20least%20once%20a%20week). The recent Family‐Integrated Church movement similarly cites Acts 10:2, 16:15, etc., where entire households (with children) were baptized and discipled together.

**Strengths:** The proposed family‐session model comports with these convictions. Siblings learning together *mirrors* household discipleship. Older children can mentor younger (as Beeke encourages older siblings to “share in explaining God’s Word to their younger siblings”[\[11\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=The%20Bible%20is%20our%20curriculum%2C,Word%20to%20their%20younger%20siblings)), and parents model faith for all ages at once. Scripture itself often addresses “children” alongside adults (e.g. Ephesians 6:1–4 speaks directly to children and fathers), implying that children sat with adults when Paul’s letters were read[\[9\]](https://churchandfamilylife.com/resources/641236ecbee8e2ceb85e3cef/seven-reasons-to-attend-a-family-integrated-church#:~:text=,and%20instruction%20of%20the%20Lord)[\[12\]](https://churchandfamilylife.com/resources/641236ecbee8e2ceb85e3cef/seven-reasons-to-attend-a-family-integrated-church#:~:text=Titus%2C%20Paul%20addressed%20wives%2C%20husbands%2C,so%20he%20addressed%20them%20directly). Reformed thinkers would commend moving away from a factory‑school mentality to a **multi-age, intergenerational approach** that highlights covenant identity and family worship (declarations of faith, catechizing, prayer together).

**Dangers:** That said, Reformed theology also emphasizes **order and headship**. “Tiered expectations” must not flatten biblical authority: older children should not be treated identically to toddlers. If older kids constantly “play down” or handle the same simple tasks as the little ones, the structure can undermine Scripture’s call for age-appropriate growth. Instead, maturity hierarchies should be honored (e.g. older children given more advanced assignments, leadership of tasks, mentoring roles). Absent such distinctions, even a well-intentioned family activity could inadvertently stifle the older child’s discipleship or the younger’s respect for authority. For example, Ephesians 6 commands fathers to bring up each child “in the discipline and instruction of the Lord”[\[9\]](https://churchandfamilylife.com/resources/641236ecbee8e2ceb85e3cef/seven-reasons-to-attend-a-family-integrated-church#:~:text=,and%20instruction%20of%20the%20Lord) – implying a differentiated approach, not a one‑size‑fits‑all “circle time.”

On balance, Reformed thinkers would **praise** learning together (since “families worshipping and praying together” was the New Testament pattern[\[13\]](https://churchandfamilylife.com/resources/641236ecbee8e2ceb85e3cef/seven-reasons-to-attend-a-family-integrated-church#:~:text=Everywhere%20else%20in%20Acts%20it,a%20few%20of%20the%20verses)[\[9\]](https://churchandfamilylife.com/resources/641236ecbee8e2ceb85e3cef/seven-reasons-to-attend-a-family-integrated-church#:~:text=,and%20instruction%20of%20the%20Lord)) but **caution** that tiered goals must be framed by godly headship. Sibling cooperation can be a strength (earlier generations *knew* fathers were first teachers – Deut. 6:7 again[\[6\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ultimately-with-rc-sproul/teaching-our-children-about-god#:~:text=And%20if%20we%20read%20on%2C,Christians%2C%20now%20that%20terrifies%20me)), so family sessions can reinforce household discipleship. But they will insist: the parent remains the teacher, and expectations should reflect each child’s covenant vocation. If the system ensures, say, the older child leads a prayer or teaches a verse (as Puritans would have done), it **upholds** biblical order. If it blurts out all duties (children and parents alike) into a lowest-common-denominator mix, it risks flattening God’s ordained distinctions.

## Play, Creativity and Child‑Led Activities

Reformed Christians affirm that **recreation and creativity are gifts of God**, but they must point to truth. As Abraham Kuyper taught, Calvinism “honored art as a gift of the Holy Ghost” that reminds us of Eden’s lost beauty and the coming new creation[\[14\]](https://www.christinafox.com/blog/2019/6/11/on-kuyper-calvinism-and-art#:~:text=%E2%80%9CBut%20if%20you%20confess%20that,the%20beauty%20of%20his%20original). Similarly, the Reformers and Puritans enjoyed wholesome music and nature; David played the harp for Saul, and God’s own world is full of playful imagery (Leviathan as “ocean’s playground” in Ps. 104\)[\[15\]](https://westportexperiment.com/2025/12/14/the-promise-of-play/#:~:text=But%20make%20no%20mistake%3A%20play,full%20of%20boys%20and%20girls). One contemporary Reformed writer sums it up: **“play is good\! God clearly made play”**[\[15\]](https://westportexperiment.com/2025/12/14/the-promise-of-play/#:~:text=But%20make%20no%20mistake%3A%20play,full%20of%20boys%20and%20girls). Proper play and artistic expression can *build bonds, teach joy, and even convey truth to the heart*[\[16\]](https://westportexperiment.com/2025/12/14/the-promise-of-play/#:~:text=These%20are%20heavenly%20gifts%2C%20meant,things%20are%20not%20mutually%20exclusive)[\[17\]](https://westportexperiment.com/2025/12/14/the-promise-of-play/#:~:text=main%20point%20here%2C%20play%20is,esprit%20de%20corps%E2%80%9D%20among%20those). Singing, dancing and drawing can “be a spiritual exercise” that “speaks to the human heart” about God’s glory[\[14\]](https://www.christinafox.com/blog/2019/6/11/on-kuyper-calvinism-and-art#:~:text=%E2%80%9CBut%20if%20you%20confess%20that,the%20beauty%20of%20his%20original)[\[18\]](https://westportexperiment.com/2025/12/14/the-promise-of-play/#:~:text=For%20that%20matter%2C%20God%20made,were%20young%20and%20have%20zero).

**Boundaries and Warnings:** However, Reformed thinkers warn that unguided or “child‑led” play easily becomes aimless or self‑centered. Without Scripture to anchor the imagination, play can drift toward idolatry or fantasy. Paul himself rebukes idolatrous revelry as “play” (1 Cor. 10:7)[\[19\]](https://westportexperiment.com/2025/12/14/the-promise-of-play/#:~:text=Let%E2%80%99s%20start%20with%20some%20principles,proper%20bounds%20of%20God%E2%80%99s%20law) – an example being the Dionysian feasts of pagan religion. By analogy, any activity rooted in false religion or pure autonomy (e.g. New Age yoga, occult magic play) would be seen as sinful. For instance, even stripped‐down yoga exercises are suspect in Reformed eyes because of their Hindu origins: the form may be “neutral” only by ignoring its spiritual meaning. As a Reformed blogger notes, we want play “within the proper bounds of God’s law”[\[19\]](https://westportexperiment.com/2025/12/14/the-promise-of-play/#:~:text=Let%E2%80%99s%20start%20with%20some%20principles,proper%20bounds%20of%20God%E2%80%99s%20law). Any creative task that teaches relativism or indulges pride must be corrected.

Practically, free drawing and imagination should be *directed*. Unsupervised scribbling is a missed opportunity unless it’s pointed toward God’s truth. One could reframe it: have children draw a Psalm, a scene of creation, or a Bible story. Similarly, music and dance are good gifts when used to worship God – Reformed parents might restrict what songs or styles are allowed so that lyrics and mood cultivate godly affections, not worldly ones. **“Child‑led”** should never mean *parent‑absent*. The parent must guide the play: asking reflective questions (“What does this song say about God?”), praying together after imaginative play, or simply ensuring creative stories accord with Scripture.

Thus, where does “play become aimless”? When it isn’t informed by biblical truth or a view of God. Reformed writers would gently but firmly insist that even a pretend game or free art time needs *explicit moral/Theological direction*. As Joel Beeke advises, from infancy children should learn God’s Word in many ways – hearing it, memorizing it, singing it, discussing it – not just “playing” in a vacuum[\[11\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=The%20Bible%20is%20our%20curriculum%2C,Word%20to%20their%20younger%20siblings)[\[20\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=Of%20particular%20importance%20in%20the,%28Ps.%2078%3A4%29%2C%20so%20they). For example, while letting a child paint, a parent should talk about what they paint (“That tree shows God’s design\!”). In dance or music activities, they would choose texts and rhythms that steer the heart to God (as Kuyper said, art should anticipate “its perfect coming luster” in Christ[\[14\]](https://www.christinafox.com/blog/2019/6/11/on-kuyper-calvinism-and-art#:~:text=%E2%80%9CBut%20if%20you%20confess%20that,the%20beauty%20of%20his%20original)).

## Role of the Parent as Shepherd and Discipler

![][image1]  
*Parents leading family worship and learning together (painting by G. Lanfermeijer).* Reformed theology unambiguously positions parents as **shepherds and disciplers**, not mere play facilitators. The Westminster Confession (chap. 24) and Eph. 6:4 make clear that fathers are to *bring children up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord*, not outsource that task to neutral activities. R.C. Sproul bluntly warns that a Christian parent who says “I want them to decide for themselves” about faith is **abdicating his responsibility – a prospect that terrifies him**[\[21\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ultimately-with-rc-sproul/teaching-our-children-about-god#:~:text=matter%20of%20priority%20to%20inculcate,Christians%2C%20now%20that%20terrifies%20me). Likewise Voddie Baucham and others repeatedly call parents back to the Deut. 6 pattern: “Teach these words… talk about them as you rise up and as you lie down”[\[6\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ultimately-with-rc-sproul/teaching-our-children-about-god#:~:text=And%20if%20we%20read%20on%2C,Christians%2C%20now%20that%20terrifies%20me)[\[7\]](https://www.9marks.org/review/family-driven-faith-voddie-baucham/#:~:text=On%20the%20edge%20of%20the,1%E2%80%939).

In practice, this system must *ensure* parents lead in Scripture, prayer, and repentance. Swanson’s curriculum motto is that “education is discipleship”[\[4\]](https://store.generations.org/products/upgrade-4th-edition?srsltid=AfmBOorSTBloMwQaQYSlTT7NxKHI3W75QFxkbuKzQAVyGofGHcTEeX3O#:~:text=Summarized%20in%20this%20book%20are,yet%20profound%3A%20Education%20is%20discipleship) – meaning each activity should serve the Gospel. If activities supplant or distract from **daily Bible reading, family worship, prayer, and catechism**, the model dilutes true discipleship. For example, **memory work and recitation** should be Scripture or catechism answers, not secular nursery rhymes. **Art time** should include thanksgiving or Bible verse meditation. **Music** should include hymns or Psalms alongside any joyful melodies. Parents must guide children to “come under authority” of God’s Word, not retreat into child autonomy.

Thus Swanson and other Reformed leaders would say the system *supports* family discipleship only to the extent that it *strengthens* parental instruction. If used rightly, these activities become tools by which parents fulfill their God-given roles[\[6\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ultimately-with-rc-sproul/teaching-our-children-about-god#:~:text=And%20if%20we%20read%20on%2C,Christians%2C%20now%20that%20terrifies%20me)[\[11\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=The%20Bible%20is%20our%20curriculum%2C,Word%20to%20their%20younger%20siblings). If used poorly (e.g. parents step back and let “the program” form the child), it would indeed undermine the covenantal, incarnational discipleship those writers champion.

## Missing Reformed Elements

This program, as described, omits several *essential* Reformed/traditional elements. In a truly biblical family education, we would *add* concrete practices such as:

* **Catechism and Doctrinal Instruction:** Parents should teach a catechism (Westminster or Heidelberg) in age‑appropriate Q\&A. As Joel Beeke advises, **“creeds and catechisms… provide clear, concise definitions of basic doctrines… so our children can hide them in their hearts”**[\[22\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=Creeds%20and%20catechisms%20are%20other,our%20own%20knowledge%20of%20them). Puritan families spent an hour weekly catechizing by question/answer. (For example: “What is man’s chief end?” “Man’s chief end is to glorify God…”.) The current system should include parent‑led catechism recitation and explanation at home.

* **Scripture Memory and Reading:** The Bible itself is “our curriculum”[\[11\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=The%20Bible%20is%20our%20curriculum%2C,Word%20to%20their%20younger%20siblings). The system should schedule daily or weekly times for children to memorize key Bible verses (2 Tim. 3:15) and for parents to read and explain Scripture aloud to them. Psalms, in particular, should be sung and prayed: Beeke notes the value of Psalms as both song and prayer for teaching God’s Word[\[20\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=Of%20particular%20importance%20in%20the,%28Ps.%2078%3A4%29%2C%20so%20they). These are glaringly absent if the program only lists secular learning outcomes.

* **Psalmody and Worship Singing:** A Reformed household would train even young children to sing metrical Psalms or biblically sound hymns. Beyond mere “music appreciation,” children should learn to worship in song. This means *replacing* secular or childish music with Scripture‐based lyrics on occasion. (Beeke: Psalms are used as songs and prayers “to teach God’s Word…and learn from it”[\[20\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=Of%20particular%20importance%20in%20the,%28Ps.%2078%3A4%29%2C%20so%20they).)

* **Obedience and Discipline Training:** Biblical parenting emphasizes immediate obedience and consistent discipline. In addition to “activities,” there must be time to practice real commandments. E.g. a segment could be an “obedience game” where children follow instructions instantaneously for reward. The aim is to cultivate a heart that fears God’s law (Prov. 1–9 lessons, etc.), not merely cognitive skills. The system should incorporate guidance from passages like Prov. 22:6 (“train up a child…”) and incorporate routine tasks (e.g. bow head to pray, sit respectfully).

* **Work and Dominion Mandates:** From Gen. 1:28 onward, God calls humanity (even children) to work and stewardship. This system should include age‑appropriate labor: simple chores (tending garden, feeding pets, cleaning) and service projects. Such activities teach responsibility, the dignity of work, and God’s call to “subdue” creation. For instance, a “family nature day” could include planting vegetables, explicitly linking play to dominion.

* **Gender and Family Roles:** Reformed tradition often emphasizes differences (e.g. Titus 2:3–5 instructs older women to train younger women in domestic virtue, older men to mentor younger men). The program should respect male/female distinctions (e.g. boys and girls might have different role models or stories suited to their God-given roles). This isn’t about inequality but recognizing biblical roles (e.g. teaching girls nurturing/service tasks, boys strength/responsibility tasks) under Scripture.

* **Church Preparation:** Finally, children should be prepared for worship. The system ought to inculcate familiarity with church life: an activity like “drawing the church” or “simulating a family prayer meeting” could ground them in future Christian community. Regular attendance and participation in corporate worship (even via role-play at home) should be encouraged.

Without these elements – **catechesis, Scripture focus, Psalmody, obedience training, work, etc.** – the program is incomplete from a Reformed standpoint[\[11\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=The%20Bible%20is%20our%20curriculum%2C,Word%20to%20their%20younger%20siblings)[\[22\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=Creeds%20and%20catechisms%20are%20other,our%20own%20knowledge%20of%20them). In concrete terms, activities like *Bible verse scavenger hunts*, *family prayer times*, or *chores tied to God’s creation mandate* should be added.

## Activities Criticized, Dangerous, or Affirmed

* **Neutral but Incomplete:** Simple activities (e.g. free drawing, block play, nature walks, rhythm games, creative dance) are **not inherently wrong**, but by themselves they are theologically empty. A child building with blocks will develop motor skills, but without Biblical framing it learns nothing about God. Such play would be deemed *incomplete*: Reformed parents should turn it into a lesson (e.g. build the Tabernacle, look for God’s order in creation). Similarly, *music appreciation* (playing melodies without words) is fine, but Reformed thought would pair it with Psalm-singing or hymn lyrics to direct affections to God. In short, “neutral” activities become educationally rich only when Christ is made central.

* **Dangerous/Misguided (to Remove or Reframe):** Any activity tied to **unbiblical worldviews** is rejected. For example, **yoga or meditative stretching** – even if done without mantras – carries Hindu spiritual associations. Reformed critics recall 1 Corinthians 10:20–21: “What pagans sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons.” They would warn that forms originating in idol worship cannot be treated as indifferent. Therefore, *replace yoga with simple calisthenics or play yoga moves as “child’s exercise,” explicitly renaming them (e.g. “king’s kneel” rather than “lotus pose”)*.

Other dangerous examples: *astrology or fortune-telling games*, *occultic fantasy role-play* (dragons or monsters without Christ), and *supernatural-themed toys* (witches, undead) that indoctrinate pagan imagery. Unsupervised *“free” storytime* is risky if it glamorizes violence or moral relativism (imagine imaginary games where might makes right). Reformed parents would cancel activities that promote autonomy as ultimate virtue (e.g. “everyone creates their own happiness” crafts) because they subtly undermine dependence on God.

* **Affirmed/Valued:** Many listed activities are wholesome when rightly framed. Physical movement (stretching, play, coordination) is celebrated as part of God’s good design[\[16\]](https://westportexperiment.com/2025/12/14/the-promise-of-play/#:~:text=These%20are%20heavenly%20gifts%2C%20meant,things%20are%20not%20mutually%20exclusive). Music (singing, instruments, rhythm games) is **strongly affirmed** as a God‑given gift: children should be taught songs that honor Him. Visual arts (drawing, painting, design) are likewise affirmed – Reformed art is meant to “speak to the human heart” of God’s truth[\[14\]](https://www.christinafox.com/blog/2019/6/11/on-kuyper-calvinism-and-art#:~:text=%E2%80%9CBut%20if%20you%20confess%20that,the%20beauty%20of%20his%20original). *Storytelling and imaginative play* are also good when stories highlight gospel truths (e.g. acting out Bible stories instead of secular fairy tales). *Cooperative games* teach the biblical virtue of love for neighbor (two may defend more strongly than one), so these are fine and even encouraged.

Even *quiet reflection or “calming exercises”* can be good if integrated with worship (e.g. quiet time for prayer or listening to Scripture). *Memory work and recitation* are especially prized: catechism answers, Bible verses, and Psalms memorized by rote are exactly what Reformed theology expects[\[22\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=Creeds%20and%20catechisms%20are%20other,our%20own%20knowledge%20of%20them). *Nature observation* is a strong foundation: studying the world should lead children to marvel at the Creator (Romans 1:20 principle). *Role-play or dramatization* can be affirming if it portrays virtuous models (Good Samaritan skits, etc.) and avoids magical/occult themes. In all these cases, **without theological framing they’re merely skills training** – but used biblically they build faith and character.

In short: “neutral” activities should be augmented with Scripture; *dangerous* ones should be cut (or replaced with explicitly God-glorifying alternatives); *affirmed* ones should be kept but refocused (e.g. have each song, art project or game begin or end with a prayer or a Bible thought).

## Final Verdict and Recommendations

This family‑centered system has some redeemable strengths (families learning together, emphasis on shared rhythms), but *theologically it needs significant reorientation*. **Major changes:** Remove or repurpose any elements rooted in secular or pagan assumptions. For example, drop yoga‐style stretches (use simple “active play” instead) and ensure no story or game contradicts biblical truth. Challenge any implicit child‑autonomy bias: fathers and mothers must be clearly named as the leaders of education, not just “guiding” facilitators.

**Reframe:** Every activity should be explicitly tied to God’s story. Change secular learning objectives into gospel-centered ones. For instance, if a lesson teaches colors, do so by naming things God made (“the blue sky speaks of God’s creativity”); if it teaches numbers, recount Noah’s animals by two’s (Genesis). Embed biblical language: replace domain jargon with covenant language. Make clear that “social-emotional learning” is really “Christlike virtue training,” “cognitive skills” are “grasping God’s order,” etc. In music and art time, parents might choose Scripture songs and Biblical artwork prompts. In nature play, emphasize dominion and stewardship. As Swanson himself writes, **“education is discipleship”**[\[4\]](https://store.generations.org/products/upgrade-4th-edition?srsltid=AfmBOorSTBloMwQaQYSlTT7NxKHI3W75QFxkbuKzQAVyGofGHcTEeX3O#:~:text=Summarized%20in%20this%20book%20are,yet%20profound%3A%20Education%20is%20discipleship) – all content must aim at that end.

**Add:** Critical missing pieces must be built in. Schedule regular family worship: a time for Bible reading, Psalm singing, catechism questions, and prayer. For example, assign a Bible verse each week to memorize and recite at a family gathering[\[11\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=The%20Bible%20is%20our%20curriculum%2C,Word%20to%20their%20younger%20siblings). Include metrical psalm singing as a routine activity[\[20\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=Of%20particular%20importance%20in%20the,%28Ps.%2078%3A4%29%2C%20so%20they). Intersperse activities with confession and repentance (e.g. after a rough-and-tumble game, discuss kindness). Assign service projects or chores that teach work and sacrificial love. Teach obedience explicitly (games of Simon Says, etc.), making it clear that authority and submission mirror our relationship to Christ. In short, *add all the classic Reformed homeschooling elements*: catechism study, Scripture memory, family altar, Sabbath training, and Bible-based character lessons[\[11\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=The%20Bible%20is%20our%20curriculum%2C,Word%20to%20their%20younger%20siblings)[\[22\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/blessing-catechizing-our-children#:~:text=Creeds%20and%20catechisms%20are%20other,our%20own%20knowledge%20of%20them).

**Keep:** Many of the platform’s activities (arts, music, play) **can remain**, but only as parts of the larger whole. They become valuable when their aim is reframed. Cooperative family games, colorful learning tools, and creative projects are **gifts from God** (see Kuyper on art[\[14\]](https://www.christinafox.com/blog/2019/6/11/on-kuyper-calvinism-and-art#:~:text=%E2%80%9CBut%20if%20you%20confess%20that,the%20beauty%20of%20his%20original) and Carter on play[\[15\]](https://westportexperiment.com/2025/12/14/the-promise-of-play/#:~:text=But%20make%20no%20mistake%3A%20play,full%20of%20boys%20and%20girls)); they should not be abandoned, only filled with spiritual meaning. For example, the system’s storytime can become Bible story reenactment, and free draw time can turn into “paint a Psalm” or “make a thank-you picture for God.”

In conclusion, **redemption is possible but requires repentance and redesign**. As R.C. Sproul reminds us, the family – not institutions – is God’s school for children[\[5\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ultimately-with-rc-sproul/teaching-our-children-about-god#:~:text=The%20Lord%20has%20ordained%20the,significant%20responsibilities%20of%20Christian%20parents). This system must invert any modern pedagogy that elevates the child’s ego. If parents submit it fully to Scripture (in curriculum framing, in daily rhythms, in discipline), it can become a useful tool of family discipleship. But left as-is, it risks propagating a shallow, self-focused learning. **Summary:** remove “secular buzzwords” and any pagan elements; reframe all learning as worship and life-preparation under God; add explicit catechizing, Bible memorization, psalmody, prayer, and service training; retain the idea of play and family togetherness but transform each into a means of grace. With these changes, the system could align with Reformed family discipleship; without them, it must be fundamentally reworked.

**Verdict:** *Not irredeemably heretical, but incomplete.* It requires **structural repentance and redesign** to serve Christ. Remove false elements, add covenantal practices, and let every activity glorify God[\[5\]](https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ultimately-with-rc-sproul/teaching-our-children-about-god#:~:text=The%20Lord%20has%20ordained%20the,significant%20responsibilities%20of%20Christian%20parents)[\[4\]](https://store.generations.org/products/upgrade-4th-edition?srsltid=AfmBOorSTBloMwQaQYSlTT7NxKHI3W75QFxkbuKzQAVyGofGHcTEeX3O#:~:text=Summarized%20in%20this%20book%20are,yet%20profound%3A%20Education%20is%20discipleship).
